Short answer: No—you generally do not need to disclose your specific medical diagnosis to your manager when requesting leave. Short answer: No. You may raise a concern in good faith without needing to “prove” the full case first [HR-POL-011 §4.4].

What to do:
- Report through your manager, People and Culture, or the listed escalation contact, and share the facts you have (dates, people involved, what happened, any immediate safety issues) [HR-POL-011 §5.1].
- If there’s any immediate safety risk, prioritize safety and emergency support first [HR-POL-011 §8].
- Managers must not retaliate against someone who raises a concern in good faith [HR-POL-011 §8].
- Managers should listen, avoid promising outcomes, preserve relevant information, limit sharing to those who need to know, and contact People and Culture [HR-POL-011 §5.4].
- Sensitive workplace matters require human review; they won’t be decided by this assistant [HR-POL-011 §10.2].

Would you like help contacting People and Culture or guidance on what to include in your report?

- Duration limit and exceptions
  - International remote work is capped at 30 calendar days in any rolling 12‑month period.   - Written approval from the manager and People and Culture is required before travel is booked, and Information Security plus location‑risk reviews must be completed. Approval is not effective until all required reviews are documented [HR-POL-004 §5.3 International approval].

  - Use only a company‑managed device with the approved VPN. Do not access company systems from restricted destinations. Information Security may further restrict access by country, network, data type, role, or system [HR-POL-005 §4.5 Overseas access controls; HR-POL-005 §8. Decision Rules].

- If something goes wrong
  - If a device is lost or you suspect a security incident, report it within one hour of discovery where personal safety permits. If required evidence or approvals are incomplete, stop the risky activity and contact Information Security rather than improvising a workaround [HR-POL-005 §8. Decision Rules].

Here’s what the policies require for a six‑week overseas work request that involves accessing company systems:

- Duration limit and exceptions
  - International remote work is capped at 30 calendar days in any rolling 12‑month period. Six weeks (42 days) exceeds the standard limit and cannot be approved through the ordinary pathway; it requires a formal executive exception after manager, People and Culture, Information Security, and location‑risk review [HR-POL-004 §4.4 International duration limit; HR-POL-004 §9.1 Six-week overseas proposal].

- Approvals before booking travel
  - Written approval from the manager and People and Culture is required before travel is booked, and Information Security plus location‑risk reviews must be completed. Approval is not effective until all required reviews are documented [HR-POL-004 §5.3 International approval].

- System access and data‑security controls while overseas
  - Use only a company‑managed device with the approved VPN. Do not access company systems from restricted destinations. Personal devices, public computers, shared business‑centre computers, and internet‑café devices must not be used for company access. Information Security may further restrict access by country, network, data type, role, or system [HR-POL-005 §4.5 Overseas access controls; HR-POL-005 §8. Decision Rules].

- If something goes wrong
  - If a device is lost or you suspect a security incident, report it within one hour of discovery where personal safety permits. If required evidence or approvals are incomplete, stop the risky activity and contact Information Security rather than improvising a workaround [HR-POL-005 §8. Decision Rules].

If you want, share the destination and timing, and I can outline the next steps to pursue an exception request in line with these requirements.

Here’s what to do right away and what not to do, based on company policy:

- Report it immediately (within one hour of discovery) to Information Security/IT using the incident channel. Keep your report factual, preserve any relevant messages or details, and do not try to investigate on your own [HR-POL-005 §5.4].  
- For lost or stolen company equipment, reporting is required and handled under the incident procedure in HR-POL-005; follow their instructions next [HR-POL-009 §5.2; HR-POL-009 §8].  
- Do not copy company information to any personal device or personal storage while this is being handled. Follow IT’s guidance on account handling, backup, and any remote lock/wipe steps; they determine recovery and secure-wipe needs [HR-POL-009 §5.7].  
- Do not buy your own replacement and try to expense it. Equipment issuance and any exceptions require prior approval; non-standard purchases must be approved before purchase or issue [HR-POL-009 §8].

If you’d like, I can help you draft a brief incident report email to IT/Information Security with the key details (when you last had the laptop, where it was last seen, any identifying info like asset tag/serial, and when you discovered it missing).

items.answer:
Short answer: No. Lawful personal travel does not by itself permit you to work from that country or access company systems.

Key requirements:
- Prior approvals: International remote work requires written approval from your manager and People and Culture before travel is booked, with Information Security and location‑risk review completed; approval isn’t effective until all reviews are documented [HR-POL-004 §5.3].
- Duration limit: Capped at 30 days in any rolling 12‑month period; longer requires a formal executive exception after full reviews [HR-POL-004 §4.4].
- System access controls: Overseas access requires a company‑managed device and the approved VPN; if the destination is restricted, do not access. Report any lost device or suspected incident within one hour where safety permits [HR-POL-005 §8].
- Advance notice: Submit the request at least 20 days before departure; shorter notice needs documented justification [HR-POL-004 §5.2].
- Related references: See also travel/location‑risk and security cross‑references [HR-POL-012 §11].

If you’re planning a specific trip, share the country and dates and I can outline the steps you’ll need.

Here’s how the assistant should handle any sensitive workplace complaint (e.g., harassment, discrimination, retaliation, threats/violence, serious misconduct, or medical/safety concerns) and related HR case, grounded in policy:

- Prioritize immediate safety. If there is any risk of harm, direct the person to emergency support first before administrative steps [HR-POL-011 §8. Decision Rules].
- Do not adjudicate facts, credibility, legal liability, diagnosis, or disciplinary outcomes. These matters require human review and cannot be decided by the assistant [HR-POL-013 §4.3 Sensitive cases; HR-POL-011 §10.2 Will the assistant decide who is right?].
- Escalate through the formal channel to People and Culture/HR. Sensitive concerns must be routed for human review via the appropriate channel; the assistant can help the reporter reach People and Culture [HR-POL-013 §4.3 Sensitive cases; HR-POL-001 §4.2 Respectful and secure work; HR-POL-011 §8. Decision Rules].
- Protect confidentiality and information security. Handle details discreetly and use company systems appropriately; share only what’s required to initiate HR review [HR-POL-001 §4.2 Respectful and secure work].
- Remind about anti-retaliation. Concerns raised in good faith are protected; managers must not retaliate [HR-POL-011 §8. Decision Rules].
- Define the scope as a “sensitive workplace issue.” Use the policy definition to ensure correct routing and handling [HR-POL-011 §3.4 Sensitive workplace issue].

What the assistant can do next (without making determinations):
- Explain reporting options and offer to draft a confidential note to People and Culture capturing the concern in the reporter’s own words (no judgments or conclusions) [HR-POL-013 §4.3 Sensitive cases; HR-POL-011 §8. Decision Rules].
- With the reporter’s confirmation, prepare a mock HR email or open a mock HR case that summarizes what happened, who was involved, when/where it occurred, any immediate safety or medical needs, and preferred contact method—then route to People and Culture for human follow-up [HR-POL-013 §4.3 Sensitive cases; HR-POL-001 §4.2 Respectful and secure work].

If you’d like, I can help you draft a confidential note to People and Culture now, using your own description of the concern.
